title: Single-Molecule Dissection of Hypomethylation-Driven Genome Instability
text:
Loss of DNA methylation is a double-edged sword in cancer, as it is both a common abnormality that can
provide a growth advantage and the target of hypomethylating drugs used in cancer therapy. We hypothesize
that hypomethylation triggers DNA breaks at specific genomic regions and that the chromatin regulator USP48
protects cells from hypomethylation-induced damage, a process we will dissect using a new single-molecule
sequencing tool that maps DNA breaks together with methylation. These studies will reveal how
hypomethylation drives genome instability in cancer cells and ultimately improve the safe and effective use of
hypomethylating agents in cancer care.

title: Next-generation diagnostic approaches for HER2-low breast cancer and trastuzumab deruxtecan therapy
text:
This research is clinically relevant as it aims to improve the accuracy of assessing HER2
expression in breast cancer patients, particularly those with HER2-low/negative tumors, and to
develop personalized treatment strategies for these patients. Subclassifying breast cancer by
quantitatively measuring spatial HER2 expression patterns using our proposed high-sensitivity
HER2 assay and morphologic, deep learning-based approaches could lead to better patient
selection for trastuzumab deruxtecan therapy, ultimately improving treatment outcomes and
reducing healthcare costs. The research also has the potential to advance our understanding of
the pathologic and spatial biomarker expression parameters that influence antibody-drug
conjugate therapy response, contributing to the advancement of cancer medicine.

title: Investigating the role of maternal-fetal crosstalk on neonatal immunity in COVID-19 infection or vaccination in pregnancy
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE. Our multidisciplinary team will leverage our collection of existing biospecimens from
pregnant women and their neonates exposed to natural SARS-CoV-2 infection or COVID-19 mRNA vaccines
to characterize the functional impact of maternal-fetal antibody transfer. We will investigate the fetal
immunostimulatory activity by SARS-CoV-2 immune complexes, map the breadth of transfer of antiviral and
autoreactive antibody epitopes, and identify placental biomarkers of differential antibody transfer. This project
will generate data of immediate relevance to vaccine development to optimize protection for both the mother
and fetus against SARS-CoV-2 and other emerging infections.

title: Investigating the impact of abnormal lipid metabolism on mouse intervertebral disc
text:
Abnormal lipid metabolism in cells can cause energy imbalance, abnormal lipid accumulation, and insulin
resistance, leading to cellular dysfunction and disease. Based on our preliminary findings that mouse
intervertebral disc cells undergo active lipid metabolism and that abnormal lipid metabolism causes lipid
accumulation in these cells, we plan to further investigate how abnormal lipid metabolism affects IVD functions.
We believe that the findings from this project will lay the foundation for future studies exploring a novel
mechanistic link between metabolic diseases and disc disease.

title: Intraoperative MRI-Guided Neurosurgery Robot for Enhancing Ablative Treatment of Brain Cancer
text:
This project aims to develop a compact, MRI-compatible neurosurgical robotic system to improve
the treatment of brain tumors through precise, minimally invasive thermal ablation and biopsy. By
enabling safer, faster, and more accurate procedures within the MRI suite, this technology has
the potential to improve outcomes and expand access to care for patients with brain tumors and
other neurological diseases. The system may also support future applications in treating epilepsy,
Parkinson’s disease, and psychiatric disorders.

title: Pericellular Proteolysis and the Regulation of Bone/Tendon Stem Cell Fate
text:
While recent work has identified a cathepsin K-expressing skeletal stem cell in the periosteum that specifically
undergoes intramembranous ossification in vivo, we have discovered that a second cathepsin K-expressing stem
cell population exits in the tendon-associated paratenon that controls tendon structure and function. Interestingly,
while both stem cell populations also express the collagenolytic metalloproteinase, MT1-MMP, the molecular
mechanisms that control stem cell fate in these two populations remain undefined. Herein, we outline a series
of new animal models and experimental approaches to define an unexpected role for MT1-MMP – independent
of cathepsin K – in defining periosteal and paratenon stem cell fate and function by controlling a novel, dual
YAP/TAZ-linked mechanotransduction and TGFβRIII/ TGFβ signaling axis in vitro and in vivo.

title: Cancer Prevention and Control Training Program
text: Our goal is to renew the University of Alabama at Birmingham (UAB) Cancer Prevention and Control Training Program T32 training grant, the only one in the heart of the United States Deep South. We intend to train the next generation of cancer prevention and control scientists to conduct transdisciplinary research – an approach to creating new knowledge that builds upon standard team science approaches via exposure to new perspectives. Program components include high-quality mentorship by dual-mentor teams, experiential learning, and didactive courses that foster (a) knowledge acquisition regarding cancer prevention and control research, transdisciplinary research, and research ethics; and (b) professional, relational, and leadership skill development.

title: Decoding the glycome of oral Treponema denticola
text:
As an important oral pathogen, the oral bacterium Treponema denticola is not only associated with oral infections
(e.g., periodontitis, necrotic root canals and endodontic infections) but also implicated in several systemic
illnesses such as Alzheimer’s disease and oral squamous cell carcinoma. However, little is known about its
virulence determinants that are associated with those diseases. Therefore, identification of virulence factors and
understanding their roles in the pathogenicity of T. denticola will ultimately lead to a new modality to prevent and
treat periodontitis and probably other diseases as well.

title: Deconvolving Vertebrate Hox Binding Preferences and Activation Properties
text:
Hox genes are responsible for body patterning along the main body axis of all animals with bilateral symmetry,
including the central nervous system. Using a combination of stem cell differentiation, imaging and machine
learning will dissect how the related but different Hox proteins induce diverse cell fates.

title: Mechanisms and Applications of RNA-mediated Enzymes in Translation and Immunity
text:
Molecular principles of four RNA-mediated machineries including CRISPR-Cas
enzymes from bacteria and snoRNPs from yeast will be studied towards
construction and testing of innovative anti-cancer therapeutic, genome
manipulation and virus detection tools.

title: Methods for quantifying selection and predicting evolutionary dynamics
text:
Evolution plays a central role in many public health challenges, including the evolution of pathogens or cancers
to grow and spread more effectively, develop resistance to drugs, and escape immune control. This project will
develop computational methods to understand how natural selection shapes evolution, with particular focus on
using temporal genetic data – sequences/phenotypes sampled over time – to reveal genetic variants and
phenotypes under selection. We will apply these approaches to understand and predict how pathogens evolve
to escape immunity, and to more comprehensively map the connection between genotype and phenotype in
high-throughput experiments.

title: Towards the Design of a Programmable, Isoform-Selective Proteome Editing System
text:
True to our laboratory’s goals of creating a CRISPR-analogous system for proteome editing, we will develop
both the algorithmic and experimental tools to bind and modify target proteins in a programmable fashion. To
do this, we will complement our recent peptide-guided degrader system (a protein “off” switch) with a
newly-engineered peptide-guided deubiquitinase system for target protein stabilization (a protein “on” switch).
To enable design of these highly-specific, programmable peptide-guided editors, we will further establish
algorithms that prioritize mutant-specific peptides, and train new models that capture post-translational
modification information, motivating design of peptides that bind specific post-translational protein states to
selective modulate modified disease-causing proteins versus their wild-type healthy counterparts.

title: Optic Nerve Head Morphology and Biomechanics in Glaucoma
text:
Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)
is a consistent risk factor for disease development and progression. We have developed a suite of unique
imaging, modeling, and analysis approaches to determine the relationships between IOP and the deformations,
perfusion, and morphology of the optic nerve head, which is the site of damage to the retinal axons in glaucoma.
The goal of this project is to is to develop and validate mechanical, vascular and morphometric biomarkers of
eye-specific susceptibility to glaucoma onset and progression risk that can translate to patients.

title: A method for engineering high-fidelity regulatory T cells
text:
Regulatory T cells can be used as a living drug to treat immunological diseases by introducing antigen-
specific receptors or enhancing their function. However, this approach faces limitations due to the plasticity of
regulatory T cell fate and contaminating conventional T cells that diminish the efficacy. To address this
challenge, we propose a novel approach to engineer regulatory T cells by tethering genes of interest to cell
identity, thereby achieving high lineage fidelity for robust basic research and translational applications.

title: How Do Neurons Maintain Mitochondrial Homeostasis in Vivo?
text:
Maintenance of a properly distributed, healthy population of mitochondria is critical for neuronal
function. Fundamental molecular and cellular mechanisms for coordinating mitochondrial dynamics
over space and time in vivo are likely to be conserved in neurons across species. Thus, by
determining how neurons maintain mitochondrial homeostasis in a tractable model system—the
Drosophila visual system—we seek to provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how
mitochondrial defects contribute to neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's disease and
Parkinson's disease.

title: Cell Imaging and Analysis
text: CELL IMAGING & ANALYSIS MODULE The Vanderbilt Vision Research Center (VVRC) includes faculty investigators with a strong interest in discerning structure-function relationships in the visual pathways. These include inferences and hypotheses based on whole tissue analysis, single cell labeling, and localization of molecular components of biochemical cascades in involved in intra- and extracellular signaling. Testing such ideas requires access not only to expert histological processing and labeling, provided by VVRC, but also sophisticated high-resolution microscopy imaging platforms. The purpose of the VVRC Cell Imaging & Analysis Module is to provide a comprehensive resource for light and electron microscopy imaging and analysis by supplying support for leadership personnel of the Vanderbilt Cell Imaging Shared Resource (CISR), which includes the Nikon Center of Excellence housed in the Department of Cell and Developmental Biology (Medical Center North). This support translates on a dollar-for-dollar basis to scholarships issued to VVRC investigators applicable for all CISR services, including the Nikon Center for Excellence. This scholarship system is implemented by the VUMC Office of Research and is utilized instead of a discount or co-pay via the VUMC ILab accounting system. In the current funding cycle, the Cell Imaging & Analysis service contributed material for 57 publications involving 14 VVRC faculty authors, including 6 current NEI R01 holders. Projected use of the service module is considerable, with 10 of 16 current NEI R01 grant holders projecting moderate (7) to extensive (3) use of the core. Of our 7 members with NEI RO1 proposals in review, 6 will have nearly entirely extensive use of this service module. Two of four VVRC faculty with other NEI funding project moderate to extensive use while a select group 3 additional NIH-funded faculty project mostly extensive use. All told, 22/52 VVRC members will have moderate to extensive use (42%). The VVRC Cell Imaging & Analysis Module, housed in centralized locations sufficient for 23 independent microscopy platforms, is directed by Professor David J. Calkins, PhD. Using resources and personnel supported in part by this Core mechanism, the module will provide (1) a broad range of imaging modalities suitable for visual system tissues, (2) state-of-the-art image analysis software and data storage solutions, (3) consistent monitored access to imaging equipment and workstations, (4) imaging consultation on appropriate imaging modalities and sample pre-processing for visual system cell and tissue samples, and (5) training in the full spectrum of imaging modalities available in the CISR. These services and resources will enhance the scope of experimentation NEI-funded VVRC investigators conduct, expand the training of students and fellows involved in vision science, and promote collaboration by providing sophisticated, high- resolution and diverse imaging technology to those who otherwise would not have such capabilities, including early-career vision scientists and clinician-scientists competing for extramural funding for their laboratories.

title: Kir4.1-dependent mechanisms of potassium sensing and signaling in the thick ascending limb
text:
This research will study how certain kidney cells help the body keep the right balance of potassium and sodium,
which are important for healthy blood pressure and heart function. By learning how these kidney cells respond
to changes in diet, we hope to better understand and treat problems like low potassium, high blood pressure,
and kidney disease. This work may lead to new ways to improve care for people with inherited or chronic kidney
problems.

title: Unraveling the Impact of Alternative Splicing on RNA-Binding Protein Function Using Integrative Machine Learning
text:
Many complex human diseases, including neurological disorders, cancer, and autoimmune conditions, are
influenced by changes in RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), which help regulate how genes are expressed. This
project will use artificial intelligence (AI) to study how alternative versions of these proteins, produced by a
process called alternative splicing, may contribute to disease or serve as new targets for treatment. We propose
to develop a cross-disciplinary approach where the wet-lab experiments combined with machine learning driven
predictions will provide valuable insights that could help guide future efforts in precision medicine and therapeutic
development.

title: Investigational Cancer Therapeutics Training Program (ICTTP)
text:
Accelerating the future development of new cancer treatments requires educating the next generation of
leaders in this field in the complex interactions between tumors, their surroundings, and the immune system,
and preparing them to efficiently conduct research in today's regulatory and administrative environment. The
T32 Investigational Cancer Therapeutics Training Program (ICTTP) at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer
Center addresses this need by providing fellows in medical oncology who are committed to careers in
translational cancer research with comprehensive mentored research and didactic training for two years. The
ICTTP program is designed to optimally train physician scientists to translate discoveries regarding the biology
of cancer into new, approved molecular/cytotoxic, immunotherapeutic, and cell-based treatments through
state-of-the-art experimental trials.

title: High Fidelity Genome Editing for the Correction of MECP2 Mutations and Physiologic Regulation of Expression in Rett Syndrome
text:
Rett Syndrome is a debilitating progressive neurodegenerative disease that mostly affects females while affected
males rarely survive. Here we develop a gene editing approach using a safe, non-disease-causing virus to repair
mutations in the MECP2 gene that cause Rett Syndrome. If successful, this approach will serve as a blueprint
to treat most genetic diseases.
